history.question: Was I really that nervous before my first half-marathon?
history.answer: You barely slept. In the July 11 conversation you said you spent the whole night staring at the ceiling with your heart racing — and at 2am you texted Alex, who answered with a voice memo promising to be at the finish line no matter what.

references.quote: I barely slept last night. Just lay there staring at the ceiling, heart racing. Ended up texting Alex at 2am and they sent a voice memo saying they'll be at the finish no matter what.

history.question: And then? How did race day go?
history.answer: On the evening of July 16 you were still standing at the finish line, medal in hand, a little in shock. Alex was there holding a ridiculous sign. You stood there for ten minutes without saying a word.

references.quote: Alex was at the finish line with a stupid sign and I just stood there for ten minutes. Didn't even say anything. Just held the medal.

history.question: How did I end up seeing the race myself?
history.answer: On July 20 you turned the whole training journey into a post — the knee injury, the pre-race panic, all of it. Reading the comments, you realized something yourself: the race was never about the time. It was about proving you could stick with something.

references.quote: the race was never really about the time. It was about proving I could stick with something.

history.question: Has your picture of me changed recently?
history.answer: Yes — the portrait keeps evolving. The newest entry sits under Traits & cognitive style: you systematically undervalue your own progress. After the half-marathon you reflexively discounted the achievement, and you were already discounting the wedding speech before giving it. The entry is anchored to two slices: the finish-line night, and your post-race reflection.

history.question: Do changes like that just happen on a whim?
history.answer: No. Every turn, five fitness buckets — card, recall, search, thinkdeep, interaction — accumulate evidence-anchored scores, and a score without your own words attached counts as zero. Only when a bucket's net drops to −5 does an evolution run actually fire; when it succeeds, that generation settles and the count restarts from zero.

history.question: What exactly does a "slice" record?
history.answer: Take the July 16 slice: its focus is "half-marathon completion and personal growth"; the emotional tone reads proud, reflective; open_loops still holds "fitness goals you might pick up next"; and the full conversation sits untouched in timeline/core.md.

history.question: Who writes those fields?
history.answer: The moment a slice closes, the turn analyzer marks it: focus, summary, tags, emotional tone. And if the model falls short that time, a deterministic fallback steps in — no slice ever closes empty.
